newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr extends retreat, morale shaky.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr extends retreat, morale shaky.

text.p: The Australian dollar extended the week's retreat to 1-3/4 cents Friday, meeting an important technical level which implied a medium term top was in place.

Today's chunk of losses came after U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan fanned rate hike speculation to fever pitch, forcing investors to face the prospect of yield differentials narrowing against the A$.

They reacted by dumping -- U.S. investment banks and Tokyo names were noteable sellers -- the dollar through US$0.7850 support to a US$0.7829 low. Asian bids helped steady it there but dealers saw risks of a deeper retracement to US$0.7750.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the currency had fled to US$0.7835/40 from an early US$0.7861/66 and US$0.7875/80 late here Thursday.
The latest lapse brought the retracement to a technically significant 38 percent of the rally from the year trough of US$0.7550 on February 12 to last week's US$0.8005 peak.

Chart watchers said a period of consolidation would normally be expected now, but conceded the prospect of a U.S. rate hike next week confused the picture and kept risks biased to the downside. Resistance was expected at the old US$0.7850 support level and the currency would have to regain US$0.7910 to reverse the bearish trend.

The currency also backtracked on the crosses with dealers reporting aggressive selling of AUD/yen from Tokyo which dragged it back to 96.56/66 yen from an early 97.20/30 and a 4-1/2 year closing high of 98.88/98 a week ago.
In trade weighted terms the currency dipped to 60.4 from 60.6 on Thursday and a lofty 61.5 last Friday.
Losses were also noteable against the Canadian dollar with dealers reckoning the Bank of Canada would come under pressure to follow any Fed tightening with one of their own.
The market has long thought the Fed would have to move sometime this year given the surprising strength of U.S. growth.
Greenspan's uncharacteristically explicit testimony on the economy today convinced many the tightening would come as early as the Fed's policy meeting next Tuesday.
He emphasised the need for the central bank to be pre-emptive and noted that if it did tighten next week the effects on inflation might not be felt until late this year.
"There were a couple of new developments in his testimony which make us think a hike is odds-on," said John Kyriakopoulos, senior economist at J.P. Morgan in Sydney.
In particular, Greenspan noted intial jobless claims stayed low in March indicating the labour market remained tight.
The chairman also noted that the percentage of households telling the Conference Board consumer confidence survey that jobs were plentiful had risen sharply of late.
That in turn, said Kyriakopoulos, suggested workers were becoming more confident about the job situation, in which case they would be less likely to accept continued low wages.
If, as expected, the Fed did hike it would probably be by 0.25 point taking the key Fed funds rate to 5.50 percent.
That would cut the gap with Australia to 0.50 point and U.S. money rates had already moved to price in a further Fed hike pairing the actual spread even more.
Dealers said this narrowing was likely to attract hot money to the U.S. currency which was seen as a far more liquid and safe investment than the Australian dollar.
Longer term a U.S. tightening was not all negative for the A$. The prospect had already added to a sharp upward shift in domestic bond yields which had seen spreads against the U.S. actually widen.

The reason for the Fed's vigilance -- a strong and growing U.S. economy -- also boded well since it promised to spill over into Europe and Japan and boost world demand for commodities, Australia's main export. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
